title: Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh
hookLine: a father and son executed in Lahore in 1745 for refusing to give up their faith

lines: A SIKH WITH A POST IN LAHORE.
A SON WITH HIS LIFE AHEAD.
cards: Some people live between two worlds. They work inside a system and belong to a community that system is hunting. They translate, they carry messages, they try to keep both sides talking.
Subeg Singh was one of those people. Tradition says he was a Sikh who held a post with the government in Lahore, trusted enough to be sent with messages to the Khalsa.
He had a son, Shahbaz Singh, a young man with his life ahead of him.

teach.b: For a while, Subeg Singh's position kept his family safe. He was useful. He was a bridge.
But the hunted years turned harder, and a bridge takes the strain from both sides. Tradition says the trouble began with the son. Shahbaz Singh was pressed to give up his faith, and he refused.
Then the father was arrested too. Both were brought before the authorities in Lahore, and both, tradition says, were offered the same thing: their lives, if they would leave the Sikh path.
What makes this story so hard to hear comes next. Tradition says the authorities did not only threaten them; they tried to use them against each other.

teach.h: THE SON REFUSES. THE FATHER IS TAKEN.
teach.b: A father can be broken through his son, a son through his father.
Surely one of them would give way to save the other.

Neither did. Tradition says they were put on the wheel, the charkhri, a torture that Sikhs name in the Ardas, the standing prayer, when they remember those who were broken on wheels and did not give up their faith.
Tradition counts Subeg Singh and Shahbaz Singh among them, together. What the tradition dwells on is not only the pain. It's the strange kind of love in it.
Either might have given his life for the other. What neither would do was ask the other to give up his faith.
They held each other up by holding on: father and son, side by side, each making the same refusal, and each, in a way, making it easier for the other.

how: Sikhs remember Bhai Subeg Singh and Bhai Shahbaz Singh among the martyrs recalled in the daily Ardas, which remembers those who were broken on wheels rather than give up their faith.

o: a Sikh general who led the Taruna Dal
a father who kept faith beside his son
a Lahore official who hunted the Khalsa

p: a Sikh with a post in Lahore

s: Subeg Singh was an outsider with no ties to the government
tradition says he held a post in Lahore and carried messages to the Khalsa.
in the tradition, the trouble began with the son
Shahbaz Singh was pressed to give up his faith and refused; then his father was arrested too.
the father gave way to save his son
neither gave way. they are remembered together.

games.q: you're Subeg Singh. your son is beside you, and you're both offered your lives if you give up your faith. what do you do?
o: give way to save your son.
urge your son to give way, to save him.
hold to your faith, as your son holds to his.
games.why: tradition says neither gave way. they were put on the wheel, and tradition counts them among the martyrs the Ardas recalls.

practice: Bring to mind a father and a son you know, maybe your own father, maybe your son, maybe a pair you've watched from a distance, close or estranged, and see them side by side.
Notice what they carry for each other, and what lies between them. If you pray, hold them before Waheguru, saying the Name on each breath out; if you don't, just wish them well, breath by breath.

wordCard.voice: Subeg Singh. A father in Lahore, offered his life to give up his faith alongside his son Shahbaz Singh; neither would, and tradition counts them among the martyrs the Ardas recalls.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: shaheed, a martyr, one who gives life rather than faith.

carryVoice: Your line: father and son. Neither one asked the other to let go of his faith. Rest gently tonight.
